title: Asking for directions
topic: giving directions in the present tense; seguir, girar, cruzar; usted
why: This lesson teaches you to ask for and understand directions: phrases for approaching someone, the route verbs (seguir, girar, cruzar, tomar) in the present tense, and ordinal numbers. It sets up the usted forms in the third person and recycles hay / está and prepositions of place, before the unit review; the imperative comes at A2.

Asking the way politely

In the street, you approach a stranger with an “excuse me,” then ask a short question. Spaniards rarely use a full sentence: ¿Para ir a…? (literally “to go to…?”) is enough, where English would say “How do I get to…?”

To…You sayEnglish
approach someone (polite)Perdone…Excuse me…
approach someone (informal)Perdona…Excuse me…
ask the way¿Para ir a la catedral?How do I get to the cathedral?
ask where it is¿Dónde está la estación?Where's the train station?
look for a shop¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?Is there a pharmacy around here?
ask the distance¿Está lejos? ¿Está cerca?Is it far? Is it close?

Perdone and perdona are imperative forms, which you'll study later: learn them as set phrases. Por aquí (around here) is a set phrase too.

Tú or usted?

English has a single “you,” but Spanish makes you choose. With an older stranger, a police officer, or in an upscale shop: usted. With someone your age, out on the street in Spain: tú is perfectly fine. With usted, the verb is in the third person singular:

Verbtúusted
seguir (to keep going)siguessigue
girar (to turn)girasgira
cruzar (to cross)cruzascruza
tomar (to take)tomastoma
llegar (to arrive, to get to)llegasllega
ir (to go)vasva
Perdone, ¿para ir al museo? ¿Está lejos?Excuse me, how do I get to the museum? Is it far?
", "

Giving directions in the present tense

English usually gives directions in the imperative (“turn right”). Spanish can do that too, but it very often uses the present tense, as if narrating the route: sigues todo recto, giras a la derecha… It's like the English “you go straight, then you turn right…” It's perfectly natural, and it's what you'll use for now.

Spanish (tú)Spanish (usted)English
Sigues todo recto.Sigue todo recto.You keep going straight.
Giras a la derecha.Gira a la derecha.You turn right.
Giras a la izquierda.Gira a la izquierda.You turn left.
Cruzas la plaza.Cruza la plaza.You cross the square.
Tomas la primera calle.Toma la primera calle.You take the first street.
Llegas a una plaza.Llega a una plaza.You come to a square.

Ordinal numbers

To count streets: la primera (1st), la segunda (2nd), la tercera (3rd), la cuarta (4th) calle. Unlike English “first,” they agree with the noun: el primer semáforo, la primera calle (primero and tercero drop their -o before a masculine noun, like buen).

Landmarks

el semáforo (the traffic light), la rotonda (the traffic circle), el cruce (the intersection), la esquina (the corner), al final de la calle (at the end of the street).

Seguir changes its e to i: sigo, sigues, sigue. Cruzar is regular: cruzo, cruzas, cruza. In Spain, people also say coger for taking a street or a bus: coges la segunda calle. In Latin America, avoid coger, which is vulgar there: say tomar.

Sigues todo recto hasta el semáforo y giras a la izquierda.You keep going straight as far as the traffic light and turn left.
", "

Understanding the answer

The hardest part is understanding the answer, which is often fast. Listen for the key words: the verb (sigue, gira, cruza, toma), the direction (derecha, izquierda, todo recto) and the landmark (la plaza, el semáforo, la iglesia).

Usted sigue esta calle todo recto hasta la plaza. Cruza la plaza y toma la segunda calle a la derecha. El museo está al final de la calle, enfrente de la iglesia.You go straight along this street as far as the square. You cross the square and take the second street on the right. The museum is at the end of the street, across from the church.
You hearIt means
Está a cinco minutos a pie.It's a five-minute walk.
Está muy cerca.It's really close.
Está un poco lejos: mejor en autobús.It's a bit far: better to take the bus.
No tiene pérdida.You can't miss it.
Hasta el final de la calle.All the way to the end of the street.

If you didn't catch everything, just ask: ¿Puede repetir, por favor? or Más despacio, por favor (more slowly, please). And to double-check: ¿La segunda a la derecha?

Use what you already know: hay for any place (Hay un banco en la esquina), está for a specific place (El banco está en la esquina), and hasta for how far to go.
